title: Dow Erases 1,100-Point Drop to Close Higher as Bargain Hunters Step In
excerpt: The Nasdaq fell more than 4% early on Wednesday in an AI-led selloff sharpened by new US tariff proposals — then recovered most of the loss, closing down just 0.62% as value stocks outperformed ahead of Thanksgiving.
body:
• The Dow Jones Industrial Average erased an intraday loss of more than 1,100 points on Wednesday to close up 164.25 points, or 0.33%, at 50,182.95, according to Reuters.
  • The S&P 500 ended down 18.31 points, or 0.25%, at 7,182.78 and the Nasdaq Composite fell 147.73 points, or 0.62%, to 23,585.80 — both well off session lows after the Nasdaq had fallen more than 4% early in the day.
  • The early selloff was driven by AI-linked stocks and new US tariff proposals on 14 trading partners; bargain hunters stepped in ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.
  • US markets are closed on Thursday for Thanksgiving and close early on Friday.

Wall Street staged a dramatic late-session reversal on Wednesday, November 25. The Dow Jones Industrial Average, down more than 1,100 points at its session low, closed higher, while the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite finished with modest losses after bargain hunters stepped in ahead of the US Thanksgiving holiday, Reuters reported.

The Dow rose 164.25 points, or 0.33%, to 50,182.95. The S&P 500 lost 18.31 points, or 0.25%, to 7,182.78, and the Nasdaq Composite lost 147.73 points, or 0.62%, to 23,585.80. Early in the session the picture had been far worse: the Nasdaq fell more than 4%, and the Nasdaq 100 briefly fell 20% from its record closing high, flirting with bear-market territory.

An AI selloff, and fresh tariff proposals

The morning selloff centered on artificial intelligence stocks. Nvidia shares fell 3.9% on the day and an index of semiconductors was off 0.7%, while Amazon fell 3.1%, according to Reuters. Technology and consumer discretionary fell 1% each and led declines among S&P 500 sectors, while materials and real estate led gainers. On the positive side, PC maker HP gained 11.5% after it reported fourth-quarter revenue and profit above analysts' estimates.

Sentiment was also hit by trade policy. The United States proposed tariffs on goods from 14 trading partners to combat what it calls structural excess industrial capacity, reviving global trade tensions. Investors were also weighing the prospect of interest rates staying higher for longer, as inflation has accelerated and oil prices have risen steadily due to the Iran war, Reuters reported. Data on Wednesday showed the US economy grew much faster than initially estimated in the third quarter while inflation increased further in October, reinforcing expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise rates next month and again in early 2027.

"There are all these potential headwinds, but then there's also a certain amount of conditioning of buying on the dip, and that's part of what we're seeing."

— Oliver Pursche, Senior Vice President and Adviser, Wealthspire Advisors

Why the market came back

Oliver Pursche, senior vice president and adviser at Wealthspire Advisors in Westport, Connecticut, told Reuters that broad selloffs tend to "throw the baby out with the bathwater," and that investors were taking advantage of the discrepancies created. Charlie Ripley, senior investment strategist at Allianz Investment Management, described the selloff as broadly sentiment-driven and said that, on a price-to-earnings basis, some companies were starting to look more attractive.

The recovery had a value tilt: value stocks outperformed growth, with the Russell 1000 value index up 0.4% and the Russell 1000 growth index down 0.8%. Advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 2.04-to-1 ratio on the NYSE. Peter Cardillo, chief market economist at Spartan Capital Securities in New York, pointed to the tariff-inflation link, telling Reuters that tariffs are "somewhat responsible for inflation... so that's actually being counterproductive to what the Fed is trying to do."

The Hindu BusinessLine noted that, despite Wednesday's recovery, the Nasdaq and the S&P 500 remained on track for their worst November since 2008; Reuters put the Nasdaq Composite down 7.3% for the month. Trading volume on US exchanges was about 22 billion shares. US markets will be closed on Thursday for Thanksgiving and will close early on Friday.
